passage:
[1] On a spring night in 1889, a delicate instrument in Potsdam, Germany, traced a small disturbance onto a strip of smoked paper. Ernst von Rebeur-Paschwitz had built the device to record the slow tilting of the ground under the pull of the moon, and the wobble that crossed his paper that night was, by the standards of his experiment, a nuisance. Only weeks later, reading a notice of a large earthquake near Tokyo, did he think to compare the clocks. The disturbance had traveled the width of the planet. Nothing in his apparatus had been designed to catch it, and that accident opens the modern study of the Earth's interior.

[2] Earthquakes send out several kinds of waves, and two of them carry the argument that follows. A pressure wave, called P, travels by compressing and stretching the rock ahead of it, much as sound travels through air. A shear wave, called S, travels by sliding the rock sideways across its own direction of motion, and it can do so only in a material that resists being deformed sideways. Both waves bend as they pass through rock of changing density, and both should reach a distant instrument at a time that can be calculated in advance, provided the interior they crossed is the interior the calculation assumed.

[3] By the turn of the century, stations across Europe, Japan, and the Americas were exchanging records, and the arrival times of one large earthquake could be assembled from dozens of them. The pattern that emerged was not the smooth one anyone had drawn. Beyond roughly 103 degrees of arc from the source, a distance measured around the curve of the globe and amounting to some 11,500 kilometers, the direct P wave stopped arriving altogether. Farther still, past about 142 degrees, it came back, late and weakened. Between those two arcs lay a band, encircling the planet, in which the direct wave was simply missing. Seismologists call it the shadow zone.

[4] In 1906 Richard Dixon Oldham argued that the shadow required a core: a sphere of markedly different material at the center, which P waves enter, slow in abruptly, and bend steeply downward, so that they surface beyond the far edge of the band rather than inside it. Beno Gutenberg put the top of that sphere at a depth of about 2,900 kilometers in 1913, a figure that a century of denser networks has since moved by only a few kilometers. Consider what kind of evidence this was. Nobody had sampled the core, and nobody has. What had been observed was an absence, in a place where a wave was expected.

[5] The S waves said something sharper still. Past that same 103 degrees, the direct S wave is missing everywhere on the far side of the planet, not late, not faint, but gone. A shear wave needs a medium that resists sideways deformation, and a liquid does not resist. That the outer core passes P waves and extinguishes S waves is the reason the textbooks call it molten, an inference drawn not from any specimen but from the failure of one kind of wave to appear.

[6] The next correction came from a record almost too faint to argue with. Inge Lehmann, who ran Denmark's seismic stations and kept her arrival times on cards in oatmeal boxes, noticed in the early 1930s that a handful of stations deep inside the shadow zone had registered weak P arrivals from a large New Zealand earthquake. Theory predicted silence there. In 1936 she proposed that a smaller sphere sits at the center of the core, dense and rigid where the material around it is not, and that a little of the wave energy turns back from the top of that sphere into the band. Her paper on the subject carries a two-character title, P'. Two decades passed before the networks were dense enough to settle the matter in her favor.

[7] The habit is worth naming. Each advance arrived as a discrepancy: a wobble belonging to no experiment, a wave that failed to appear where it was due, a signal too weak to belong to anything. The interior of the planet has been mapped almost entirely from the gap between what the instruments recorded and what a simpler Earth would have produced.

[8] Modern arrays have not so much changed that habit as sharpened it. Hundreds of stations working together can now resolve structure only a few kilometers across at the boundary between the mantle and the core, and what they find there is not the clean surface of the textbook diagrams but patches in which waves slow far more than the models allow. Whether those patches are pooled melt, or a chemically distinct layer, or something stranger still, is argued over in the same way the core itself once was, from arrivals that a simpler picture cannot produce.
prompt: The main idea of the passage is that:
choices: improvements in the sensitivity of instruments, more than changes in theory, can account for each discovery about the planet's interior.
the boundary between the mantle and the core has proved more complicated than the early models allowed.
the interior of the Earth has been mapped largely from arrivals that a simpler picture of the planet could not produce.
seismologists could not agree, from the first distant recordings onward, about what lies at the center of the planet.
correct_answer: the interior of the Earth has been mapped largely from arrivals that a simpler picture of the planet could not produce.
explanation: The passage moves from a wobble that belonged to no experiment, to a wave that stopped arriving, to a signal too weak to belong to anything, and the seventh paragraph names the pattern outright: the interior has been mapped “from the gap between what the instruments recorded and what a simpler Earth would have produced.” Instruments open the passage, but what is credited is the reading of the records rather than “improvements in the sensitivity of instruments”; that “the boundary between the mantle and the core has proved more complicated than the early models allowed” is the subject of the last paragraph alone; and the one disagreement reported is about those patches, not about “what lies at the center of the planet.”

prompt: According to the passage, the shadow zone became visible as a pattern only once:
choices: instruments sensitive enough to register distant earthquakes had been built across Europe.
the arrival times of one large earthquake could be assembled from dozens of stations.
the top of the core had been placed at a depth known to within a few kilometers.
the pressure wave and the shear wave could be told apart on a single record.
correct_answer: the arrival times of one large earthquake could be assembled from dozens of stations.
explanation: The third paragraph makes the exchange of records the condition: stations “were exchanging records, and the arrival times of one large earthquake could be assembled from dozens of them,” and only then does “the pattern that emerged” appear. Sensitive instruments existed by 1889, before any pattern was seen; “the top of the core” was placed at a depth in 1913, after the shadow zone had already been described; and the passage never treats telling the two waves apart “on a single record” as the step that revealed the band.

choices: a wave that can cross only a material resisting sideways deformation fails to appear beyond it.

prompt: The passage indicates that Rebeur-Paschwitz connected the disturbance on his paper to an earthquake only after he:
choices: obtained records made the same night at stations far closer to Tokyo.
read a notice of a large earthquake and compared it against his clocks.
rebuilt his device to register faster motions of the ground.
found the same wobble repeated on later strips of his smoked paper.
correct_answer: read a notice of a large earthquake and compared it against his clocks.

prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that Lehmann accounted for the faint arrivals deep inside the shadow zone by proposing that those waves had:
choices: traveled the whole way inside the mantle and never entered the core at all.
come from a second and smaller earthquake that no distant station could register.

prompt: As it is used in the phrase “can now resolve structure only a few kilometers across,” the word resolve most nearly means:
choices: distinguish.
settle.
dissolve.
determine.
explanation: The sentence is about what hundreds of stations working together can see at the mantle-core boundary, structure “only a few kilometers across,” so the word carries the sense of telling small features apart. To “settle” fits the argument the paragraph goes on to describe rather than the seeing, “dissolve” attaches to the melt in the same sentence but not to what the arrays do, and “determine” would say the arrays fix what the patches are, which the paragraph explicitly leaves open.
